working_title: Electric vs Push Golf Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: A practical, opinionated guide aimed at the regular UK walker who is weighing up whether to upgrade from a push trolley to electric, or buying their first trolley altogether. The post cuts through the feature noise by anchoring every decision to real UK course conditions: hilly parkland, muddy links winters, small car boots, and club storage rooms.
research_notes:
- Push trolleys are lighter, cheaper, and need no charging; electric models are heavier due to battery and motor hardware but that weight is largely irrelevant once the trolley is rolling on course
- Key push trolley appeal: more built-in storage as standard (phone, balls, tees, umbrella holder, drink holder often included without add-ons); simpler to maintain; no risk of arriving with a flat battery
- Three-wheel push trolleys track straighter than two-wheel pull models, and pushing is easier on the body than pulling (reduces upper-body strain and twisting)
- Electric trolleys use a battery-powered motor; on hilly courses or for golfers with back or joint issues they are a material upgrade, not just a luxury
- Battery sizing matters for UK golfers: 18-hole lithium covers a standard round; 27- or 36-hole batteries suit hilly courses or back-to-back rounds
- Lithium batteries are lighter and last longer than lead-acid alternatives
- Compact fold is an important electric trolley consideration: the battery makes the unit heavier to lift, so ease of fold matters for loading/unloading
- Follow and remote models (e.g. Stewart Golf Q Follow in the £1,600–£1,900 range; Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote) are the top tier; handle-steered electric models (e.g. Motocaddy S1, PowaKaddy FX1) are the sensible entry point
- UK brand landmarks: PowaKaddy leads UK electric market with FX and CT ranges; Motocaddy is the other dominant UK brand; Stewart Golf is UK-built; Hill Billy Terrain is a budget UK-built electric option
- Push trolley price anchors found in research: PowaKaddy Micra around £189; Stewart R1-S around £159–£189; Motocaddy Cube Push at the more affordable end
- Electric price anchors: entry electric (e.g. Motocaddy SE) cited around £499; mid-range (PowaKaddy FX1 36-hole) around £549; compact fold models (PowaKaddy CT6) around £749; GPS premium (Motocaddy M5 GPS) in the £850–£1,000 range
- Some electric models add GPS with tens of thousands of courses pre-loaded, plus shot-tracking; push trolleys cannot do this
- Push trolleys easier to store at the club or in a small car; electric trolleys increasingly compact but still generally larger
- Course type is the single most useful filter: flat/municipal = push trolley often sufficient; hilly/undulating parkland or links = electric earns its money
- Foot/hand brakes on push trolleys important on sloped courses to stop bag rolling away
